meanings.note: Agrees with the thing owned. Core Russian det meaning 'my, mine' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: Where's my toy car?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'to the newlyweds' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Я, как человек щедрый, дарю лучший подарок молодожёнам.
examples.trans: As a generous man, I am giving the best gift to the newlyweds.

examples.text: На кухне ресторана всегда есть молодожёны.
examples.trans: In the restaurant kitchen there is always to the newlyweds.

meanings.note: + infinitive. Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'can, to be able', paired with 'смочь'.

examples.trans: I can't today.
That can't be.

examples.text: Этого не может быть. Это наша история.
examples.trans: That can't be. It's our history.

meanings.note: наш, наша, наше, наши; agrees with the noun

examples.trans: I love our town.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'простой'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('no ordinary / complex').

examples.text: Это непростой кирпич, а внутри золотой слиток.

examples.text: Шеф говорит, что это очень непростой выбор.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('huge, enormous').

examples.trans: Our chances are huge.
Thank you so much!

examples.text: Кстати, если хочешь, иди к нам в команду. Шансы у нас огромные.
examples.trans: By the way, if you want, join our team. Our chances are huge.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'one', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Нам очень дорого обходится авторская кухня.
examples.trans: Auteur cuisine costs us very dearly.

examples.text: Это все, кто выходил из отеля.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to her', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

meanings.note: Prefix 'под-' ('under, up to') indicates approaching or supporting from below (stem 'арок'). Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common masculine noun meaning 'present, gift' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: This is a present for you.
Thank you for the present!

examples.text: Это семейный праздник. Как в детстве, с подарками!
examples.trans: It's a family holiday. Like when we were kids, with presents!

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'здравление'). Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'congratulations / birthday wishes' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Виктория Сергеевна, примите от нас поздравления с днём рождения!
examples.trans: Viktoria Sergeyevna, accept our birthday wishes!

examples.text: На кухне ресторана всегда есть поздравление.
examples.trans: In the restaurant kitchen there is always congratulations.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'wish', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.text: Дима, привет, спасибо большое за поздравление!
examples.trans: Dima, hello, thank you very much for the birthday wish!

examples.text: Что тут, выход на пенсию отмечают?
examples.trans: What is this here, are they celebrating a retirement?

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'ехать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to arrive (by vehicle)', paired with 'приезжать'.

examples.trans: Which car did you come in?
Pasha has arrived.

examples.text: Вика, ты на какой машине сегодня приехала?
examples.trans: Vika, which car did you come in today?

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'сутствие'). Common neuter noun meaning 'presence' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: В его присутствии было некое мельфо.
examples.trans: In his presence was simply not proper.

examples.text: На нашей кухне уже есть новое присутствие.
examples.trans: In our kitchen there is already a new presence.

meanings.note: 'это просто' = it's easy. Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.
Это просто = it's easy. Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: I'm just tired.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: short form only: рад, рада, радо, рады; no long-form cases

examples.text: Ну что ты? Я очень рад тебя видеть.
